item.title: Ollama Tool Definitions Are Not Free: The Measured Prompt-Token Cost of Every Tool You Register
item.description: On Ollama 0.20.3 with qwen3:0.6b a tools block adds about 58 fixed prompt tokens before the first definition and about 57 more per terse tool, against about 292 for a verbose one — so twelve terse tools spend 746 of a 4096-token default window before the user types. Eight measured cells, three identical repeats each, raw JSONL and the aggregation script published.
item.content:encoded:
You register twelve tools on a local agent, send a six-word message, and prompt_eval_count comes back at 764 instead of 18. Nothing is wrong: the definitions you sent are part of the prompt, and on a 4k default context that registry has already spent 746 of your 4096 tokens before the conversation starts — and it re-pays that cost on every turn.

This article measures the cost instead of estimating it. One model, one fixed message, one local server, tool sets of 0, 1, 3, 6 and 12 definitions in a deliberately terse form, and sets of 1, 3 and 6 in a deliberately verbose form, three repeats per cell, with the raw request and response records published next to the script.

The short answer: a terse definition costs about 57 prompt tokens on this model, a verbose one about 292, and a non-empty tools block costs a fixed ~58 tokens of scaffolding on top of the chat template. The useful part is not the average — it is that both terms are linear, so you can compute your own registry’s standing cost from your own schemas before running anything.

What prompt_eval_count actually counts

Ollama reports the prompt size of each /api/chat response as prompt_eval_count, documented as the “Number of tokens in the prompt” (chat API reference). That number is not the length of the message you typed; it is the length of the fully rendered prompt after the chat template is applied, which is why the no-tools baseline in this fixture is 18 tokens for a six-word message.

The tools field is documented as an “Optional list of function tools the model may call during the chat” (chat API, tools parameter), and each entry is a function definition carrying a name, a description and a JSON Schema parameters object (tool calling documentation). What the documentation cannot tell you — because it is model- and template-specific — is how many tokens that object becomes once it has been rendered.

That gap is the whole problem. A schema is authored in JSON, billed in tokens, and the conversion rate depends on the tokenizer of whichever model you pulled. The argument shapes themselves are ordinary JSON Schema objects, so nested objects and additionalProperties behave exactly as the JSON Schema object reference describes — and, per the numbers below, as expensive as they are elaborate.

Method

The fixture is a single driver, tool_schema_token_audit.py, run against a local Ollama 0.20.3 server on a 2 vCPU / 11 GB container with no GPU. The model is qwen3:0.6b at Q4_K_M. Every request uses the same user message (“Reply with the single word: ready.”), stream: false, temperature: 0, num_ctx: 8192 and num_predict: 8, and differs only in the tools array.

There are eight measured cells: terse sets of 1, 3, 6 and 12 tools, and verbose sets of 1, 3 and 6, plus a 0-tool baseline. Sets of N always use the first N of twelve fixed tools, so the cells are nested and the slope across 1/3/6/12 is attributable to the added definitions and nothing else. A terse definition is a name, a one-line description and flat string or number arguments; a verbose definition carries a 110-word description plus a nested options object with an enum, numeric bounds, defaults and additionalProperties: false. Both forms are published in tool-fixture.json so the comparison can be inspected rather than taken on trust.

Two deviations from the research plan are recorded here rather than smoothed over. First, three repeats per cell were collected instead of five. The first request of a cell is the one that pays model load, and its rate is quoted here as prompt tokens per wall-clock second: the records carry total_duration_ns and the driver’s wall_s, not prompt_eval_duration (the API reports that field in its example response, but the fixture driver does not record it), so that denominator includes model load and the 8-token generation the fixture asked for, and these figures are completion rates rather than prompt-evaluation throughput. On this CPU host the first requests of the six tool-bearing cells other than the 6-tool verbose one ran at 5.8 to 13.0 prompt tokens per wall-clock second (144 tokens in 24.9 s for one terse tool, 764 in 58.9 s for twelve), the 6-tool verbose cell ran at 38.8, and the no-tools baseline falls outside that band at 0.9 prompt tokens per wall-clock second (18 tokens in 19.2 s). The stage budget did not allow five such cold requests for every cell. Second, the verbose 12-tool cell was not measured: its prompt — an extrapolated 3.6k tokens — exceeded the driver’s 260-second client timeout (REQUEST_TIMEOUT, overridable with --timeout). The attempt is kept as a timeout row with no count (TimeoutError: timed out, n_ok=0 in the published JSONL and CSV), and the run then stopped at the driver’s own deadline guard before the cross-surface cell, so no completion for that request exists in the record. The driver published beside this article catches a timeout, prints error=<type>, moves to the next cell and still writes the summary, so a rerun on a slower host degrades instead of ending early. Everything else in the tables below is a measured value, and every repeat returned an identical prompt_eval_count, so each range is degenerate and each median is an exact repeat rather than an average.

The measured numbers

Terse definitions, three repeats per cell, identical across repeats:

Tools registered prompt_eval_count Added over previous cell Per added tool
0 18 — —
1 144 +126 126
3 250 +106 53
6 415 +165 55
12 764 +349 58

The first tool is not like the others, and that is the first thing worth understanding. Going from no tools to one tool costs 126 tokens; each additional tool after that costs 53 to 58. The difference is a fixed block the template emits as soon as tools is non-empty — a preamble, an instruction line and the array scaffolding — before the first definition is serialised.

A least-squares line through the 3, 6 and 12-tool cells has a slope of 57.3 tokens per terse tool and an intercept of 75.5 at zero tools, which decomposes against the 18-token baseline into roughly 57.5 tokens of tools-block scaffolding plus 57.3 tokens per definition. That model predicts 133 tokens for a single tool against 144 measured: an 11-token residual at the smallest count, where the tokenizer’s share of the array framing is largest. The straight line through the 3- and 12-tool cells alone gives 57.1 per tool and an intercept of 78.7, so the construction matters less than it looks — the scaffolding term lands between 57 and 61 tokens and the slope between 57.1 and 57.3.

What a verbose description costs

The same twelve tools rewritten with a 110-word description and a nested options object:

Tools registered Terse Verbose Difference Difference per tool
1 144 383 239 239.0
3 250 965 715 238.3
6 415 1844 1429 238.2
12 764 not measured — —

The description cost is stable at roughly 238 tokens per tool and the verbose slope is 292.3 tokens per definition with a 71.8-token preamble at zero tools, so the verbose form is about five times the terse form and does not drift with tool count. If you were assuming a long, careful tool description is nearly free because the model “needs” it, the fixture says otherwise: one paragraph of guidance per tool is roughly 240 tokens of every turn, which at twelve tools would be nearly 2900 tokens of standing cost — an extrapolation from the measured 6-tool cell, not a measurement.

A rougher sizing rule comes out of the same rows: at twelve terse tools the set runs about 4.8 bytes of JSON per token (3558 bytes for 746 tokens) and the verbose set about 6.3 bytes per token (11531 bytes for 1826 tokens). The ratio is only usable once the fixed scaffolding is amortised, because that part does not scale with bytes: applied below the cell where it was derived, it predicts 357 tokens where 397 were measured at six tools (10% low), 171 against 232 at three (26% low) and 50 against 126 at one (61% low). For a registry of roughly six tools or more it is good enough to decide whether the set fits; for one or two tools, use the two-term formula below.

The cross-surface question stays open

Ollama’s OpenAI-compatible endpoint also accepts tools and stream_options.include_usage (OpenAI compatibility), so usage.prompt_tokens is available as a second accounting surface. That cell was not collected in this run: the run ended at the 12-tool verbose timeout before the cross-surface step was reached, and no honest comparison exists without it. The compatibility table is a support matrix, not a statement that both surfaces count tokens identically, and nothing here should be read as one — the question of whether /api/chat and /v1/chat/completions agree on the same tools payload is listed as unmeasured.

What this means for a small window

Ollama’s documented defaults choose the context length from total VRAM: 4k below 24 GiB, 32k at 24–48 GiB, 256k at 48 GiB and above (context length). This host sits in the first tier, so the denominator here is 4096 — the same default a laptop or a small CI runner gets.

At 4096 tokens, twelve terse tools are 18.2% of the window and the 12-tool verbose registry would be roughly 87% on the extrapolated slope, which is not a context budget but a context ceiling reached before the first user message. At 32k the same twelve terse tools are 2.3%. That is why “just raise num_ctx” is popular, and also why it is the wrong first lever on the small tier: the tier is chosen by VRAM, and raising num_ctx on a small host moves the cost from the prompt into the KV cache.

The arithmetic to run on your own registry is one line — 57.5 + 57.3 × tools for terse definitions, 71.8 + 292.3 × tools for verbose ones — added to whatever your template costs. Twelve terse tools is about 745 tokens; twelve verbose ones about 3579.

Decision rules that follow from the numbers

Trim before you cut. Converting twelve verbose tools to terse saves about 2800 tokens (3579 against 745), more than deleting ten of twelve terse tools would save (about 570). Rewriting descriptions is the highest-leverage edit available and changes nothing about what the model can do.

Cut when the registry itself is the problem. On a 4k window with 2k of conversation, twelve terse tools leave about 1350 tokens of slack; a third registry is not affordable and no amount of description trimming fixes that. Splitting an agent into two six-tool registries costs a second prompt and a second model load but holds each turn’s standing overhead near 415 tokens instead of 764.

Do not expect prompt caching to make the tools block free. prompt_eval_count reports what was evaluated, and a cached prefix is reported separately where the server supports it — this fixture’s single-turn requests recorded no cached count at all. Even a cheap-to-evaluate tools block still occupies the window, because context capacity and prompt evaluation cost are two different budgets and tools spend the first one whether or not they spend the second.

Reproduce it

The fixture is published: the driver script, the twelve tool definitions in both forms, the raw per-request JSONL with request hashes and prompt_eval_count, the aggregation script that turns that JSONL into the summary CSV, and the CSV itself.

  • tool_schema_token_audit.py
  • tool-fixture.json
  • fixture-raw.jsonl
  • aggregate_fixture.py
  • fixture-summary.csv

Run python3 tool_schema_token_audit.py --out <empty dir> --repeats 3 against any Ollama server and you get the same table for your own model, because the script sends the definitions verbatim and records what the server reports rather than what a tokenizer is expected to do. Give it a fresh output directory each time: the driver appends to fixture-raw.jsonl, so a second run into the same directory mixes two runs into one summary. python3 aggregate_fixture.py --raw fixture-raw.jsonl --csv fixture-summary.csv rebuilds the summary from whatever records exist, one row per cell, with the columns surface,cell,tool_count,n_ok,n_attempts,median,min,max,full_range,tools_json_bytes,errors — the failed 12-tool verbose cell is kept as a row with n_ok=0 and its error string, because a dropped cell would hide the most expensive result. On a slow host expect the same timeout this run hit: the first request after each tools-set change is the cold one, and the 12-tool verbose cell can exceed the 260-second client timeout before it produces a count.

What these numbers do not cover: other models, other quantisations, other templates. prompt_eval_count is tokenizer-specific, and a different chat template can move both the preamble and the per-tool slope. The values here are one model on one host on 2026-11-12 — a measurement of that configuration, not a constant of Ollama.

If you are sizing the wider agent cost equation rather than the tool term alone, the browser MCP snapshot cost analysis does the same accounting for page snapshots. If you are still deciding how to structure the calls themselves, the function calling guide covers the mechanics, and the Ollama API integration guide documents the surrounding request surface.

item.title: vLLM Tool-Call Streaming: Detecting Corrupted Arguments
item.description: Three vLLM reports filed in October 2026 show merged, truncated and dropped tool-call arguments at different version scopes. Here is how to localize the fault and gate execution.
item.content:encoded:
A streaming tool call can reach your agent corrupted while every SSE frame on the wire is valid JSON. The damage shows up after reassembly: two calls fused into one, an argument string cut mid-token, or a number that became the string "3". The request returns HTTP 200, finish_reason says tool_calls, and an agent that trusts the payload executes the wrong thing. The practical question is not whether vLLM is “broken” in general; it is whether the corruption is in the server’s parser or in your client’s reassembly, and how to stop execution until that is settled. This article separates what the current primary reports actually establish, shows how to localize the fault with a raw SSE capture, and ships a small gate that refuses any call whose arguments do not round-trip against your declared schema.

What the three October 2026 reports actually establish

The first report is vllm-project/vllm#64012, filed 2026-10-27 and still open. It is explicitly a legacy-version report: the reporter confirms the failure on vLLM 0.19.0 with vllm/tool_parsers/qwen3xml_tool_parser.py at SHA256 7c2ba229b0b6dcd061b9f581390a5fb892a2fc20023b20656d91706522f311bd, states that the v0.19.1 source is byte-identical, and says the reproduction needs no GPU, weights, tokenizer or network. Two independent <tool_call> blocks parse correctly when they arrive in one chunk or when the split falls between the calls. When a chunk holds the first call’s closing tags plus the opening of the second, the same concatenated text produces malformed JSON and can truncate a string value. The reporter adds that #45003 removed the old XML parser and #45413 introduced newer engine routing, and calls this “the legacy v0.19.0 implementation, not an asserted regression on current main.” That boundary matters: reading this thread as evidence about v0.32.x is a version error.

The second report, vllm-project/vllm#63983, is a different failure and a different scope. It was filed 2026-10-27 and closed as completed on 2026-11-02 with no closing comment, so read the report as evidence of what the parser did, not as an open ticket. Against main at commit 5d35ce3, with parser code only and no GPU, the functiongemma parser extracts arguments written as key:<escape>value<escape>. FunctionGemma’s own chat template wraps only strings that way; numbers, booleans, arrays and objects are emitted bare, never match the parser’s regex, and are silently dropped. The issue’s printed output makes the consequence concrete: a set_alarm call carrying hour:7, enabled:true, days:[mon,tue] and snooze:{minutes:5} comes back as {"label": "Wake up"}. The call “succeeds” with four of its five arguments missing.

The third, vllm-project/vllm#63941, concerns Kimi K3 at main commit cd9aa5b5ee (2026-10-26), also parser-level and CPU-only. When a generation is cut inside an XTML control marker by max_tokens, the non-streaming path returns the raw partial marker text as user-visible content, while the streaming path withholds the same fragment. The two paths disagree about the same tokens. The reporter notes that current main tip 6fe3d447ac does not touch kimi_k3_tool_parser.py.

Report Version scope Symptom What the report does not show
#64012 v0.19.0 legacy qwen3_xml Merged/truncated arguments when a chunk straddles two calls Any regression on current releases; v0.19.1 was never executed
#63983 main @ 5d35ce3, functiongemma Non-string arguments silently dropped Chunk-boundary behaviour; other parser families
#63941 main @ cd9aa5b5ee, Kimi K3 Non-streaming leaks a partial XTML marker that streaming withholds That the leak affects schema-valid calls or other parsers

Read together, the three reports support a failure class, not one release-wide defect: chunk-boundary merge and truncation in a legacy parser, silent argument loss in one current parser, and stream/non-stream divergence in another. No single tag is shown to carry all three symptoms, and none of the reports is a measurement of your deployment. The adjacent Ubicloud write-up is often cited alongside them and should not be: it measured schema accuracy, not chunk boundaries. It reports 92% schema accuracy serving Kimi K2.6 on vLLM 0.28 against the 2,000-request K2VV ToolCall workload, 100% after constrained decoding was enabled as a vLLM 0.31 server flag, and a drop to 91% when a later release changed the default. That is a constrained-decoding story about argument validity, and it is useful context for why strictness flags exist. It is not evidence that streaming splits corrupt calls.

The flag semantics that matter, pinned to v0.32.0

The current stable release on 2026-10-28 is v0.32.0 (published 2026-10-18), followed by v0.31.0 and v0.30.0, according to the release list. The tool-calling documentation pinned to that tag defines the startup flags plainly: --enable-auto-tool-choice is mandatory for automatic tool choice, --tool-call-parser selects the parser, --tool-parser-plugin optionally registers a custom one, and --chat-template is optional. It also states the division of labour that this article is about: “Remember that it’s the caller’s responsibility to … Handle the tool calls in your application logic.” The server flags choose and drive a parser; they do not certify the arguments your application is about to execute.

The same page documents the strictness behaviour that changed the risk picture in this release line. Structural tags constrain the tool-call envelope (markup and function name) always for tool_choice="required" and named calls, and for tool_choice="auto" only once a tool sets strict: true or the server raises the floor. Argument schemas are pinned only for tools marked strict: true, or under --tool-strict-level parameter. The --tool-strict-level values are auto (default, follow the request), function (constrain envelope for every request with tools), and parameter (pin every tool’s argument schema). VLLM_ENFORCE_STRICT_TOOL_CALLING defaults to true and, when false, disables structural tags entirely. The page names the reason a gate is still needed: with tool_choice="auto" and no strict tools, “the model generates tool calls without any grammar and malformed markup can leak into the response.”

Parser coverage is version-specific too. The v0.32.0 page lists FunctionGemma under functiongemma and Kimi-K2 under kimi_k2; the string kimi_k3 does not appear on that page at all. So the Kimi K3 defect in #63941 is a main-branch parser report, not a documented v0.32.0 parser you can select by reading this page.

Localize the fault before you patch anything

Three checks separate a server parser defect from a client reassembly defect, and they take minutes rather than a GPU rental.

First, capture the stream verbatim. curl -N --no-buffer with your normal request body, redirected to a file, preserves event framing, data: lines and chunk order. Second, replay that capture through the exact buffering code your agent uses, splitting the captured bytes at every offset. A client that decodes each TCP read independently will fail inside multi-byte characters; a client that trims whitespace or re-serialises arguments will fail on types. Third, send the same prompt non-streaming and compare the resulting calls. If the raw deltas concatenate to valid JSON and the non-streaming call matches, the fault is client-side reassembly. If the raw deltas themselves are invalid or short, the fault is upstream of your client. If both parse but disagree on types or call count, suspect the parser or the model’s chat template rather than transport.

The gate published with this article includes that boundary replay as a selftest. It builds a five-event stream carrying two parallel calls, serialises it as OpenAI SSE frames, and re-runs reassembly plus validation at all 760 byte offsets. All 760 splits reassembled without a false rejection, which is the property you want before you trust a gate to tell you that a real corruption is real. That number comes from the run record in this article’s evidence directory; it is a fixture check, not a vLLM measurement.

A gate that runs before dispatch

The gate is deliberately boring: reassemble the stream the way the OpenAI-compatible client does, parse each arguments string as JSON, then compare the parsed object with the schema the model was given. It fails closed on five conditions - unparseable JSON, non-object arguments, missing required fields, a JSON type that does not match the declaration, and a call count that differs from what the request expected. Types are compared exactly, because Python’s bool is a subclass of int and because accepting "3" where integer was declared is precisely the silent retyping a coercing client can produce.

def validate(calls, tools, expected_calls):
    issues = []
    if expected_calls is not None and len(calls) != expected_calls:
        issues.append(("CALL_COUNT_MISMATCH", f"{len(calls)} of {expected_calls}"))
    for call in calls:
        spec = tools.get(call["name"])
        try:
            args = json.loads(call["arguments"])
        except ValueError:
            issues.append(("ARGUMENTS_NOT_JSON", call["name"])); continue
        for name in spec.get("required", []):
            if name not in args:
                issues.append(("MISSING_REQUIRED", name))
        for name, value in args.items():
            declared = spec["properties"].get(name, {}).get("type")
            if declared and type_name(value) not in declared:
                issues.append(("TYPE_MISMATCH", f"{name}={value!r}"))
    return issues

Call it on the assembled message, before any tool dispatcher or agent loop sees it. On a rejection, log the raw arguments string and the finish_reason, return the errors to the model as a tool result if your loop supports that, and retry. Do not coerce values to make the call pass: coercion converts a detected type error into an undetected wrong argument, which is the failure this gate exists to prevent.

The published selftest exercises four constructed corruptions derived from the clean fixture, and each is caught by a distinct code rather than by a generic exception:

Constructed corruption Detected as Calls reassembled
Two calls merged into one delta ARGUMENTS_NOT_JSON + CALL_COUNT_MISMATCH 1 of 2
Arguments cut mid-string ARGUMENTS_NOT_JSON 2
Integer, boolean, array re-encoded as strings TYPE_MISMATCH 2
Non-string arguments dropped MISSING_REQUIRED 2

Two limits follow from the design. A merged call cannot be reconstructed, only rejected, so the correct recovery is a retry with the error surfaced, not a repair heuristic. And a schema-valid but semantically wrong argument - the failure class Ubicloud measured - passes the gate by definition; strict decoding and a stronger schema are the tools for that, not this check.

What is verified, what is not

Everything about the three reports above was re-read from the GitHub API on 2026-10-28 between 12:01:39 and 12:01:43 UTC, the window recorded in the research fetch log for this article, and the pinned documentation and release list were fetched inside that same window. The gate and its fixtures were executed in the same session, and the run record captures the command, exit code, stdout and input hashes. What was not done matters just as much: vLLM is not installed in this workspace image, so no parser was imported and no claim is made that any listed defect reproduces at v0.32.0. The reports’ own commits and version labels are quoted as the reporters stated them. There is no throughput, latency, cost or accuracy measurement here, and no claim that all vLLM parsers are affected - the matrix is one legacy parser, one current parser family and one current stream/non-stream divergence.

If you operate a vLLM endpoint for an agent, the operational order is: pin the tag you actually run, capture one streaming and one non-streaming response with parallel calls, replay the capture at every byte boundary through your client, and enable the gate before the next deploy. If the corruption survives that sequence at a pinned tag, you have a reproducible parser report to file rather than an intermittent symptom to describe.

Sources

Primary sources, all re-fetched on 2026-10-28 UTC:

  • #64012, legacy qwen3_xml chunk-boundary report - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/64012
  • #63983, FunctionGemma non-string argument drop - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/63983
  • #63941, Kimi K3 stream/non-stream marker leak - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/63941
  • Published releases and dates (v0.32.0 latest stable in this window) - https://api.github.com/repos/vllm-project/vllm/releases?per_page=6
  • Tool-calling flags, strict mode and --tool-strict-level, pinned to v0.32.0 - https://docs.vllm.ai/en/v0.32.0/features/tool_calling.html
  • Adjacent schema-accuracy measurement (different failure class; not chunk boundaries) - https://www.ubicloud.com/blog/fixing-tool-call-accuracy-in-vllm

First-party artifacts published with this article (constructed fixtures, no model output; local fixture check, not vendor measurement):

  • Gate and boundary selftest - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baeseokjae/baeseokjae.github.io/main/research/evidence/vllm-streaming-tool-call-parser-corruption-2026/toolcall_gate.py
  • Parallel-call SSE fixture - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baeseokjae/baeseokjae.github.io/main/research/evidence/vllm-streaming-tool-call-parser-corruption-2026/fixtures/sse_parallel_toolcalls.json
  • Declared tool schema used by the gate - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baeseokjae/baeseokjae.github.io/main/research/evidence/vllm-streaming-tool-call-parser-corruption-2026/fixtures/tool_schema.json
  • Run record: command, exit code, stdout, input hashes - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baeseokjae/baeseokjae.github.io/main/research/evidence/vllm-streaming-tool-call-parser-corruption-2026/first-party-fixture-run-2026-10-28.json

For the argument shapes a parser is supposed to produce, see LLM function calling and tool use; for why this serving stack was chosen before parsing became the concern, see vLLM vs Ollama in production and local model serving frameworks compared.

item.title: Best LLM for AI Agents 2026: GPT-5.5 vs Claude Opus 4.7 vs Gemini 3.1 Pro on Tool Use and Reasoning
item.description: Which LLM is best for AI agents in 2026? Benchmark-by-benchmark comparison of GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, and Gemini 3.1 Pro on tool use, reasoning, and c...
item.content:encoded:
There is no single best LLM for AI agents in 2026 — Claude Opus 4.7 leads tool orchestration and code tasks, GPT-5.5 dominates terminal-style agentic workflows, and Gemini 3.1 Pro wins on context window and cost. Your model choice should follow your use case, not a global ranking.

The LLM-for-Agents Landscape in 2026 (What Changed)

The LLM-for-agents landscape changed fundamentally between 2024 and 2026, and the old question — “which model is smartest?” — has been replaced by a more precise one: “which model performs best on the specific agentic task I’m building?” As of May 2026, 31% of enterprises have at least one AI agent running in production, led by banking and insurance at 47%. Despite this momentum, 88% of enterprise AI agent pilots never reach production — with evaluation gaps (64%), governance friction (57%), and model reliability (51%) cited as the top blockers. The global enterprise AI agent spend is tracking a $1.4 trillion 2027 forecast, and the broader LLM market may reach $35.4 billion by 2030 at a 36.9% CAGR. What’s driving adoption is not a single breakthrough model, but an ecosystem shift: agentic frameworks (LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK), standardized tool protocols (MCP, function calling schemas), and multi-model routing that lets teams assign the right model to each task rather than betting everything on one provider.

Three models dominate production agentic deployments in 2026: OpenAI’s GPT-5.5, Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.7, and Google’s Gemini 3.1 Pro. Each leads a different category of benchmarks. No single model tops every leaderboard — and if you’re choosing one model to rule your entire agent stack, you’re already behind.

The Real Contenders: GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, and Gemini 3.1 Pro

The three frontier models competing for agentic workloads in 2026 are GPT-5.5 (OpenAI), Claude Opus 4.7 (Anthropic), and Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google DeepMind) — not GPT-6, which has not been released. Each represents a different architectural philosophy and strength profile. GPT-5.5 was optimized for agentic terminal workflows, CLI automation, and web browsing tasks. Claude Opus 4.7 was tuned heavily for multi-turn tool use, code generation, and instruction-following in long agentic chains. Gemini 3.1 Pro was designed for high-context reasoning tasks, offering a 2M+ token context window at a price point below $2/$12 per million input/output tokens — the lowest of the three frontier models. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, GPT-5.5 leads with a score of 60, while Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro are tied at 57. On LMArena (human preference voting), Claude Opus 4.7 topped the leaderboard as of late April 2026. These divergences aren’t noise — they reflect genuinely different strengths that matter at the task level.

Quick Spec Comparison

Model Context Window Input Price Output Price Strength
GPT-5.5 256K tokens ~$5/M ~$20/M Terminal agents, web browsing
Claude Opus 4.7 200K tokens ~$15/M ~$75/M Tool use, code, long chains
Gemini 3.1 Pro 2M+ tokens <$2/M <$12/M Long-context reasoning, cost

Tool Use & Function Calling Benchmarks — Who Actually Wins

Tool use and function calling performance is the most important benchmark category for agentic systems, and the 2026 results reveal a clear stratification. Claude Opus 4.7 leads the MCP-Atlas tool orchestration benchmark at 77.3–79.1%, compared to GPT-5.5 at 75.3% and Gemini 3.1 Pro at 73.9%. On tau-bench retail — a rigorous multi-turn tool use benchmark that simulates real customer service agent workflows — Claude Sonnet 4.5 (Anthropic’s smaller model) leads at 0.862, 3.8 points ahead of the next model. For cost-sensitive, high-volume function calling pipelines, Gemini 3.1 Pro’s price-performance ratio wins.

The Multi-Model Architecture: The 2026 Production Pattern

The multi-model agent architecture — routing different tasks to different LLMs within a single agent system — is the dominant production pattern in 2026, and the data supports why. No single model leads every relevant benchmark: Claude Opus 4.7 wins on code and orchestration, GPT-5.5 wins on terminal workflows and web research, Gemini 3.1 Pro wins on context and cost. Teams that bet on a single model sacrifice 10–20% performance on tasks where a different model leads. The winning architecture uses a lightweight router (often a smaller model or a rule-based system) that classifies each task and dispatches it to the appropriate specialist. A common pattern: Claude Opus 4.7 for code generation and multi-step tool orchestration, GPT-5.5 for web browsing and terminal tasks, Gemini 3.1 Pro for document-heavy analysis and cost-sensitive high-volume calls. This requires more infrastructure — multiple API integrations, fallback logic, unified logging — but the performance and cost benefits at scale make it the rational choice. With 81% of enterprises planning to expand into more complex agent use cases in 2026, multi-model routing is quickly becoming the baseline expectation, not an advanced optimization.
